Time in view for a circular viewing area

Source: R/availability.R
view_window.Rd

Computes the window for availability() when the observers watch a circular area around the platform, fore and aft alike. The window is the time a point on the water spends inside that circle as the platform passes. For an aircraft side window use view_window_aerial(); for a ship's forward search use view_window_vessel().

Usage

view_window(radius, speed, distance = 0)

Arguments

radius

Numeric. Radius of the viewing area, in metres. Must be positive.

speed

Numeric. Platform ground speed, in metres per second. Must be positive.

distance

Numeric. Perpendicular distance, in metres. Default 0, the trackline, which gives the widest window. Must not be negative.

Value

A numeric vector of windows in seconds, 0 where distance exceeds radius.

How it works

For a viewing radius \(r\) and platform speed \(v\), a point at perpendicular distance \(x\) is crossed along a chord of length \(2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\), so

$$w(x) = \frac{2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}}{v}$$

The window is widest on the trackline, shrinks with distance, and is 0 beyond the radius.

Which platform this fits

Only a platform that watches a circular area. An aircraft observer looking through a side window sees a wedge running forward and aft, so time in view grows with perpendicular distance instead of shrinking; this function gets that direction wrong. Ganley et al. (2019) measured time in view rising with distance for their aircraft, at about 0.03 s per metre. A window measured in the field, as they did by timing a buoy through the field of view, is better than any of these formulas.

References

Ganley, L.C., Brault, S. and Mayo, C.A. (2019) What we see is not what there is: estimating North Atlantic right whale Eubalaena glacialis local abundance. Endangered Species Research 38:101-113. doi:10.3354/esr00938 Time in view measured for an aircraft, rising with perpendicular distance.

See also

view_window_aerial() for an aircraft, view_window_vessel() for a ship, and availability() for what the window feeds.

Examples

# A 300 m viewing radius at 50 m/s, on the trackline
view_window(radius = 300, speed = 50)
#> [1] 12

# The window narrows away from the trackline and is 0 beyond the radius
view_window(radius = 300, speed = 50, distance = c(0, 150, 290, 400))
#> [1] 12.000000 10.392305  3.072458  0.000000
